Vargha and Delaney's A (Stochastic-Superiority Effect Size)

Source: R/vargha_delaney_A.R
vargha_delaney_A.Rd

Takes two independent samples of scores that can be ordered and returns Vargha and Delaney's (2000) A, the probability that a randomly drawn observation from the first population exceeds a randomly drawn observation from the second (a tie counting one half), with its standard error, a confidence interval, and a test of \(A = 1/2\). The statistic uses only the order of the observations, so it needs no assumption of normality or of equal variances and suits ordinal and skewed outcomes.

Usage

vargha_delaney_A(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  ci_method = c("logit", "wald"),
  test = c("t", "permutation", "z"),
  exact = NULL,
  n_resamples = 10000L,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

x

Either a numeric or logical vector of observations from group 1, an ordered factor, or a two-sided formula of the form outcome ~ group (in which case data must be supplied and the grouping variable must have exactly two observed levels; its first level is group 1). Two ordered factors must have the same levels in the same order. An unordered factor and a character vector are refused; see What is refused, and why.

y

Observations from group 2, of the same kind as x. Ignored when x is a formula.

data

Optional data frame containing the variables named in the formula x.

conf_level

Confidence coverage for a symmetric interval (default 0.95).

ci_method

Either "logit" (default; Wald interval on the logit of A with back-transformation, which keeps the limits inside (0, 1)) or "wald" (untransformed Wald on the original scale, clipped to [0, 1]).

test

Reference distribution of the test of \(A = 1/2\). "t" (default) refers \((\hat A - 1/2)/\mathrm{SE}\) to Student's t with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the test of Brunner and Munzel (2000). "permutation" refers the same statistic to its distribution over reassignments of the scores to the two groups (a studentized permutation test; Neubert and Brunner, 2007). "z" refers it to the standard normal distribution. See The test.

exact

Logical. If NULL (default), the permutation test enumerates every reassignment when choose(n_1 + n_2, n_1) is at most 50,000 and samples reassignments otherwise. If TRUE, enumeration is forced (refused above 1,000,000 reassignments). If FALSE, random reassignments are forced. Used only when test = "permutation".

n_resamples

A single whole number of at least 1: the number of randomly drawn reassignments when enumeration is not used. Default 10000L. Used only when test = "permutation".

seed

Optional integer seed for the randomly drawn reassignments. Default NULL, under which the reassignments are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for reproducibility. When a seed is supplied the RNG state in place before the call is restored on exit. Used only when test = "permutation".

Value

A one-row data.frame (classes dmar_vargha_delaney_A and dmar_tbl) with these columns, in this order:

A

The estimate \(\hat A\).

se

Its standard error, the square root of the placement variance of DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988); 0 when the estimated variance is 0.

ci_lower, ci_upper

The confidence limits at conf_level, formed as ci_method says. Both equal A when the estimated variance is 0, and are then not a confidence interval.

test_statistic

The test statistic \(W = (\hat A - 1/2)/\mathrm{SE}\), the same under each choice of test; the test column names the distribution it is referred to. The column has this one name under all three tests. NA when the estimated variance is 0, except under test = "permutation", where it is Inf or -Inf for completely separated groups and 0 when every score is equal.

p_value

The two-sided p-value of \(A = 1/2\) (stochastic equality) from the reference distribution named in test. NA when the estimated variance is 0, except under test = "permutation".

n_1, n_2

The numbers of non-missing observations in the two groups.

ci_method

The interval method used.

df

The Satterthwaite degrees of freedom under test = "t"; NA under the other two tests and when the estimated variance is 0.

test

The reference distribution used: "t", "permutation", or "z".

The table carries these attributes: conf_level, which the console prints beneath the table and results_sentence reports; n_missing, the numbers of missing values removed from the two groups, as c(group_1 = , group_2 = ); interval_degenerate, present only when the estimated variance is 0, with the value "complete_separation" or "no_variation"; and resampling, present only under test = "permutation", a list with exact (whether every reassignment was enumerated), n_arrangements (choose(n_1 + n_2, n_1)), and n_resamples_used (the number of reassignments compared). The tidy() and glance() verbs (see dmar_tidiers) give the row in their column convention, with df and test after p_value and a logical column interval_degenerate.

Details

Estimand and interval. For independent observations \(X\) from the first population and \(Y\) from the second, $$A = \Pr(X > Y) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\Pr(X = Y).$$ The sampling units are the \(n_1 + n_2\) individuals, each observed once and each in one group. The interval is a large-sample (Wald) confidence interval for the population A, formed on the logit scale by default. A value of \(A = 0.5\) is stochastic equality, and \(A > 0.5\) says that the first group tends to score higher. Stochastic equality (Vargha & Delaney, 2000, p. 102) is weaker than equality of the two distributions: populations that differ in spread or shape can have \(A = 0.5\). The test reported here is of \(A = 0.5\). It is not a test that the distributions are identical, the null hypothesis of the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test (pp. 108–109). Qualitative magnitude labels for A are not reported, in keeping with the DMAR convention of reporting effect sizes as numbers with confidence intervals.

Assumptions. The two samples are independent of each other and the observations within each are independent and identically distributed; for paired observations use probability_of_superiority_paired. The response is at least ordinal. The estimate needs nothing more: no distributional shape, no equality of variances, and ties are allowed. The standard error, the interval, and the t and z tests are large-sample results; The test and When the estimated variance is zero say how they behave in small samples.

Scale and missing values. A depends only on the order of the observations (Vargha & Delaney, 2000, pp. 101, 107), so any increasing rescoring of the response gives the same value, and an ordinal response may be supplied as an ordered factor. Missing values (NA and NaN) are removed group by group; the numbers removed are in the n_missing attribute. Infinite values are ordered as usual. Dates and date-times (classes Date and POSIXct) are ordered by their numeric values, as are two time differences (class difftime) in the same units. A one-column matrix and a one-dimensional array are read as the vectors they are. Each group needs at least two non-missing observations; with fewer the function stops, since no variance can be estimated.

What is refused, and why. The statistic uses the order of the observations and nothing else, so the function must be given objects whose order is the order meant. It refuses, with a condition of class dmar_scores_not_ordered (see dmar_metadata), an unordered factor (its codes follow the order of levels(), alphabetical unless set, so the levels low, mid, high are stored as 2, 3, 1, and A computed from the codes of the example in Examples is 0.406 where the ordered levels give 0.656); a character vector (strings sort alphabetically, "10" before "9"); an ordered factor beside anything that is not an ordered factor with the same levels in the same order (each factor numbers its own levels from 1); time differences in different units, or one beside plain numbers (each such object is stored in its own units); a Date beside a POSIXct; and a list, data frame, or matrix of several columns. Nothing is computed in any of these cases. The message says which case applies and what to supply: an ordered factor with its levels from lowest to highest, factor(x, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"), ordered = TRUE), or numeric scores.

Sample estimate. With \(\bar R_X\) the mean rank of the first sample in the pooled ranking, mid-ranks for ties, $$\hat A = \frac{\bar R_X - (n_1 + 1)/2}{n_2}$$ (Vargha & Delaney, 2000, Equation 14, p. 107). Equivalently, \(\hat A = U / (n_1 n_2)\), with \(U\) the Mann-Whitney statistic that counts the pairs with \(X_i > Y_j\) and half of the tied pairs. The function computes the mean rank form, whose rounding can differ from the exact ratio \(U/(n_1 n_2)\) in about the thirteenth decimal place.

Standard error. Define the placements $$V_{10}(X_i) = \frac{1}{n_2}\sum_{j} \psi(X_i, Y_j), \qquad V_{01}(Y_j) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i} \psi(X_i, Y_j),$$ with \(\psi(x, y) = 1, \tfrac{1}{2}, 0\) as \(x > y, =, <\). The variance estimate is $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat A) = \frac{S^2_{10}}{n_1} + \frac{S^2_{01}}{n_2},$$ where \(S^2_{10}\) and \(S^2_{01}\) are the sample variances (divisors \(n_1 - 1\) and \(n_2 - 1\)) of the \(V_{10}\) and \(V_{01}\) placements. This is the placement (structural components) estimator of DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988, p. 840) for the area under a single receiver operating characteristic curve; Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025) state that the variance estimator of Brunner and Munzel (2000) is identical to it. It is consistent for two independent samples from any pair of distributions, with no parametric or equal-variance assumption. It is not unbiased in general: its expectation exceeds the variance of \(\hat A\) by \((\xi_{11} - \xi_{10} - \xi_{01})/(n_1 n_2) \ge 0\), where \(\xi_{11}\) is the variance of \(\psi(X, Y)\) and \(\xi_{10}\) and \(\xi_{01}\) are the covariances of two values of \(\psi\) that share their \(X\) or their \(Y\). The excess is zero when both variables take only two values. With three continuous observations per group from one distribution the variance is 7/108 and the estimator averages 8/108.

Confidence interval. ci_method = "logit" (the default) forms a Wald interval for \(\mathrm{logit}(A) = \log\{A/(1-A)\}\) with the delta method standard error \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat A)/\{\hat A(1 - \hat A)\}\), $$\mathrm{logit}(\hat A) \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2}\, \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat A)}{\hat A(1 - \hat A)},$$ and transforms the two limits back with the inverse logit, so they stay inside (0, 1). Pohar Perme and Manevski (2019) conclude that the DeLong variance estimator is reliable and that the interval should be formed on the logit scale. ci_method = "wald" returns \(\hat A \pm z_{1 - \alpha/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat A)\), clipped to \([0, 1]\). Both intervals use the normal quantile, whatever test is.

Relation to Cliff's delta. \(A = (\delta + 1)/2\), and because \(\mathrm{arctanh}(2A - 1) = \mathrm{logit}(A)/2\), the logit interval here and the interval of cliff_delta are the same construction on the two scales. The two functions estimate the variance differently, however (placement variances here; there the sample version of Feng and Cliff's, 2004, Equation 2, which has a third term), so their limits are not the same after the change of scale. For x = 1:5 and y = 3:7, \(\hat A = 0.18\) with logit limits 0.034 and 0.576, which are \(-0.931\) and 0.151 on the scale of \(\delta\); cliff_delta() gives \(\hat\delta = -0.64\) with limits \(-0.935\) and 0.177.

The test. The statistic is $$W = \frac{\hat A - 1/2}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat A)},$$ reported in test_statistic. The three choices of test share this statistic and differ in what it is referred to. "t" gives \(p = 2\,\Pr(T_f \ge |W|)\) for Student's t with $$f = \frac{\left(S^2_{10}/n_1 + S^2_{01}/n_2\right)^2} {\dfrac{(S^2_{10}/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \dfrac{(S^2_{01}/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}$$ degrees of freedom, reported in df. The statistic, the degrees of freedom, and the rejection rule are those of Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025, Equations 3 and 7, the display that precedes Equation 8, and Equation 8), written here in placement variances; they present them as the test of Brunner and Munzel (2000), whose statistic is their Equation 4.8 (p. 21) and whose degrees of freedom are their Equation 5.9 (p. 22), an approximation they recommend for group sizes of at least 10. "z" gives \(p = 2\,\Phi(-|W|)\). "permutation" recomputes \(W\) for reassignments of the \(n_1 + n_2\) pooled scores to groups of sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\): every one of the choose(n_1 + n_2, n_1) reassignments when there are at most 50,000 (or when exact = TRUE), and n_resamples randomly drawn ones otherwise, by the rules of randomization_test. The p-value is the share of reassignments with \(|W_b| \ge |W|\) under enumeration, and \((1 + r)/(1 + m)\) with \(r\) such reassignments among \(m\) random ones. A reassignment whose estimated variance is 0 has \(W_b = 0\) when its \(\hat A\) is 1/2 and \(W_b\) infinite, with the sign of \(\hat A - 1/2\), otherwise. Neubert and Brunner (2007, p. 5195) define only the one-sided p-value of their studentized permutation test, the share of reassignments whose statistic is at least the observed one, with the variance recomputed for each. Schüürhuis et al. describe its two-sided p-value as twice the smaller tail share; the form used here, the share at least as extreme in absolute value, is the one randomization_test() uses, and the two can differ. The permutation test is exact when the two distributions are equal, since every reassignment is then equally likely, and approximate when they differ in spread or shape with \(A = 1/2\).

The z reference rejects a true \(A = 1/2\) too often in small samples, which is why it is not the default. Rejection rates at a nominal .05 with normal data and \(A = 1/2\), from this function (10,000 samples per row for z and t, Monte Carlo standard error about .002; 2,000 samples for the permutation test, standard error about .005, with 399 random reassignments where the reassignments were not enumerated); the ratio is the standard deviation of the first group over that of the second:

\(n_1\)\(n_2\)SD ratioztpermutation
551.086.071.047
10101.073.056.047
8201.080.062.045
20201.060.052.046
553.084.068.048
10103.079.051.052
8203.090.062.063
2083.065.052.034
20203.062.050.052

Over these and the other simulations run for this function, which include five-category ordinal and lognormal data and group sizes from 5 to 30, the rates were .056 to .099 for z, .049 to .071 for t, and .032 to .063 for the permutation test. The t reference removes most of the excess from 10 per group upward and part of it below that. These ranges describe the conditions that were run. With one group of 5 or fewer and the other five or more times larger, the t reference rejected a true \(A = 1/2\) in .07 to .11 of samples when the two distributions were equal (.073 with 5 and 25, .085 with 4 and 20, .112 with 3 and 30; normal data, 20,000 samples each), where the permutation test is exact (the z reference rejected in .105, .124, and .172 of the same samples). When the smaller group has fewer than about 6 scores, test = "permutation" is therefore the test to use, unless the two groups also differ greatly in spread, the case described next. When the small group also had five or six times the standard deviation of the large one, so that the distributions were not equal, the permutation test rejected in .08 of samples with 5 and 25 and in .11 with 4 and 20 (4,000 samples each, 999 reassignments). When the groups are completely separated the estimated variance is 0 and only the permutation test gives a p-value: \(W\) is infinite, and the p-value is the share of reassignments that are also completely separated (2/252 for 5 and 5 untied scores).

The test and the default interval are separate procedures. The interval is formed on the logit scale so that it stays inside 0 and 1, and the test is on the scale of A. They can disagree in small samples: for x = c(3.5, 5, 6, 7, 8) and y = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4.2), \(\hat A = .92\), the logit interval is [.486, .993], the t test gives p = .0033, and the exact permutation test gives p = .032. A test on the logit scale would agree with the interval but rejects far too rarely (.007 to .041 at a nominal .05 in simulation) and is not offered.

When the estimated variance is zero. Two kinds of data give a variance estimate of exactly 0, and they are the only two. Complete separation: every observation in one group exceeds every observation in the other, so the estimate is at the end of its range (\(\hat A\) 0 or 1). No variation: every observation has the same value, so the estimate is 0.5. In both, the two limits are reported equal to the estimate under either ci_method, se is 0, test_statistic and p_value are NA (under test = "permutation" the test is reported, as described above), the table's interval_degenerate attribute names the case, and a warning of class dmar_interval_degenerate is given whose reason element is "complete_separation" or "no_variation"; the condition also carries estimate, n (the two group sizes), and limit_feng_cliff. The reported limits are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage. The zero describes the sample: the variance estimate measures how much the comparisons differ from one observation to the next, and without overlap they do not differ. Complete separation is common when the effect is large and the samples are small. With five observations per group from normal populations, it occurred in 19 percent of samples when the population value of A was 0.86 and in 59 percent when it was 0.96, and across all samples the reported 95 percent limits then covered the population value 79 and about 40 percent of the time, against 98 and 96 percent among the samples that were not separated (20,000 simulated samples each). Feng and Cliff (2004, p. 324, Equations 6 to 8) treat this case by assuming the largest variance \(\hat\delta\) can have, which gives the limit \((n_b - z^2)/(n_b + z^2)\) when \(\hat\delta = 1\) (and its negative when \(\hat\delta = -1\)), with \(n_b\) the smaller group size; they describe the result as conservative. On the scale of A that limit is \(n_b/(n_b + z^2)\) when \(\hat A = 1\) and \(z^2/(n_b + z^2)\) when \(\hat A = 0\): 0.566 and 0.434 at the 95 percent level with five in the smaller group. The warning states that limit. It is not the limit this function reports.

Particular cases. Infinite values are ordered like any others, so a group made up of Inf beside finite scores is completely separated, and two groups made up of the same infinite value have no variation. Two constant groups at different values are completely separated. Groups that only touch, the largest score of one equal to the smallest of the other, are not separated: the tied pair gives a positive variance and an ordinary interval, which is wide (c(3, 4, 5) against c(1, 2, 3) gives \(\hat A = 0.944\) with limits 0.475 and 0.997). The mark travels with the result: results_sentence writes the estimate and says that there is no confidence interval, the printed table says so beneath itself, tidy() and glance() carry it in the column interval_degenerate, randomization_test passes on the warning of cliff_delta, and ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity counts a separated replication as one without an interval. The randomization test remains valid in both cases.

Relation to other measures. A is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) when the scores are used to tell the two groups apart, and \(\hat A = U/(n_1 n_2)\) for the Mann-Whitney U. Cliff's \(\delta\) is \(2A - 1\). The common language effect size of McGraw and Wong (1992), as cles computes it, is \(\Phi(\delta/\sqrt{2})\) with \(\delta\) the standardized mean difference, which is \(\Pr(X > Y)\) for normal distributions with a common variance; A estimates that probability (with ties split) without those assumptions.

Reading the output. In the second example below the first level of treatment, Control, is group 1, with 246 children against 64. \(\hat A = 0.429\): a randomly drawn control child has the higher iq_8 than a randomly drawn child from the bloomer group with estimated probability .43, ties counting one half. The 95 percent logit interval is [0.351, 0.511], and the t test of \(A = 1/2\) has \(W = -1.72\) on 92.5 degrees of freedom, p = .089.

References

Brunner, E., & Munzel, U. (2000). The nonparametric Behrens-Fisher problem: Asymptotic theory and a small-sample approximation. Biometrical Journal, 42(1), 17–25. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1521-4036(200001)42:1<17::AID-BIMJ17>3.0.CO;2-U

DeLong, E. R., DeLong, D. M., & Clarke-Pearson, D. L. (1988). Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: A nonparametric approach. Biometrics, 44(3), 837–845. doi:10.2307/2531595

Feng, D., & Cliff, N. (2004). Monte Carlo evaluation of ordinal d with improved confidence interval. Journal of Modern Applied Statistical Methods, 3(2), 322–332. doi:10.22237/jmasm/1099267560

McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1992). A common language effect size statistic. Psychological Bulletin, 111(2), 361–365. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.111.2.361

Neubert, K., & Brunner, E. (2007). A studentized permutation test for the non-parametric Behrens-Fisher problem. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 51(10), 5192–5204. doi:10.1016/j.csda.2006.05.024

Pohar Perme, M., & Manevski, D. (2019). Confidence intervals for the Mann-Whitney test. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 28(12), 3755–3768. doi:10.1177/0962280218814556

Schüürhuis, S., Konietschke, F., & Brunner, E. (2025). A new approach to the nonparametric Behrens-Fisher problem with compatible confidence intervals. arXiv, 2504.01796. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01796

Vargha, A., & Delaney, H. D. (2000). A critique and improvement of the CL common language effect size statistics of McGraw and Wong. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 25(2), 101–132. doi:10.3102/10769986025002101

Examples

# Two numeric vectors.
set.seed(113)
x <- rnorm(40, mean = 0.6)
y <- rnorm(40, mean = 0)
vargha_delaney_A(x, y)
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df    
#>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0082  40  40  logit     77.962
#>  test
#>  t   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Formula interface on the pygmalion field experiment. The first factor
# level (Control) forms group 1, so A below 0.5 says a randomly drawn
# control child tends to score below a child from the bloomer group.
vargha_delaney_A(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion)
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df    
#>  0.429 0.041 0.351    0.511    -1.718         0.0892  246 64  logit     92.478
#>  test
#>  t   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Wald (untransformed) interval rather than logit.
vargha_delaney_A(x, y, ci_method = "wald")
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df    
#>  0.666 0.061 0.546    0.786    2.712          0.0082  40  40  wald      77.962
#>  test
#>  t   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The studentized permutation test and the normal reference. With
# 40 per group the reassignments are sampled, so a seed is given.
# n_resamples = 2000 keeps the example quick; a reported p-value
# deserves the default of 10,000.
vargha_delaney_A(x, y, test = "permutation", n_resamples = 2000,
                 seed = 113)
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df  
#>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0120  40  40  logit     <NA>
#>  test       
#>  permutation
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Permutation test: 2000 random reassignments
vargha_delaney_A(x, y, test = "z")
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df  
#>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0067  40  40  logit     <NA>
#>  test
#>  z   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# An ordinal response is supplied as an ordered factor with its levels
# stated from lowest to highest. The unordered factors rating_1 and
# rating_2 themselves are refused, with a message that says why: their
# codes follow the alphabetical order of the labels (high, low, mid).
rating_1 <- factor(c("low", "mid", "high", "high"))
rating_2 <- factor(c("low", "low", "mid", "high"))
lev <- c("low", "mid", "high")
vargha_delaney_A(factor(rating_1, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE),
                 factor(rating_2, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE))
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df test
#>  0.656 0.209 0.237    0.921    0.748          0.4827  4   4   logit     6  t   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Completely separated groups: the estimated variance is 0, the two
# limits equal the estimate, and a warning says that they are not a
# confidence interval. The permutation test still gives a p-value, the
# share of the 252 reassignments that are also completely separated.
separated <- vargha_delaney_A(6:10, 1:5, test = "permutation")
#> Warning: vargha_delaney_A(): the groups are completely separated (A = 1), so the estimated variance is 0. Both confidence limits are reported equal to the estimate (1, 1). They are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage: the variance estimate is built from how much the comparisons differ from one observation to the next, and in a sample with no overlap they do not differ at all. That describes this sample, not the population. A population with some overlap often produces a sample with none when the samples are small (here 5 and 5 observations), so the limits must not be read as showing that the population value is 1. For this case Feng and Cliff (2004, Equation 8) give the limit (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for delta = 2A - 1, with n_b the smaller group size and z the normal quantile of the level: 0.131 here at the 95% level, with the other limit 1; on the scale of A, 0.566, with the other limit 1. The permutation test is reported (test_statistic is infinite); the t and z tests are not defined here. Report the estimate with the sample sizes and say that the groups did not overlap; the randomization test (randomization_test()) gives a p-value that remains valid here.
separated
#>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df  
#>  1.000 0.000 1.000    1.000    Inf            0.0079  5   5   logit     <NA>
#>  test       
#>  permutation
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Limits are not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0.
#> 
#> Permutation test: all 252 reassignments
results_sentence(separated)
#> [1] "A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0), unadjusted p = 0.0079"
